To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the OPP-method can be further improved by a) exploiting the polynomial structure of integrands at multiple cut-conditions and by b) using the DFT to perform a projection.
the reduction of one loop amplitudes in QCD can be improved significantly, and that the resulting reduction algorithm is very versatile and can be applied to a variety of processes.

the reduction of one loop amplitudes can be performed more efficiently by exploiting the OPP-method, that the projection-technique can be used to efficiently reconstruct the polynomials, and that the method is applicable to the calculation of NLO QCD processes.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the reduction of one loop amplitudes to a basis of master integrals, in the context of NLO QCD calculations for processes with multiple electroweak gauge bosons in the final state, and the implementation of the reduction procedure in the automated framework GoSam.
the development and implementation of efficient methods for computing one- and multi-loop amplitudes, with the ultimate aim to compute NLO QCD and NLO EW corrections to processes at hadron colliders.
the development of efficient methods for the evaluation of one-loop amputated amplitudes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the reduction algorithm is now very efficient in practice.

the reduction of one loop amplitudes in the context of multi-loop calculations is a non-trivial problem and that the OPP-method, while being a great improvement over the traditional methods of reduction, still has some shortcomings.
the new reduction algorithm is a significant improvement over the standard OPP method, and is competitive with the more recent OPP+ methods.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the reduction algorithm is now completely automated, and can be applied to any amplitude with a number of external legs and particles in the loop.
the reduction of a one-loop amplitude to master integrals is now possible in a completely automatic and efficient way.

the number of integrals to be computed numerically is reduced by 50% with respect to the standard approach, and that the number of numerical integrations needed to reconstruct the polynomials is reduced by 90%.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the reduction of a one-loop amplitude can be performed in a fully automatic and fast manner.
the number of master integrals is reduced by a factor of 2, which leads to a significant speed-up of the calculation.
the number of required integrals is reduced by a factor of two, compared to a conventional reduction, while the number of required terms is only slightly increased.
